NASA's Artemis III crew begins final training

Published 2026-10-06 09:30 UTC

NASA's four Artemis III astronauts have begun their final phase of training before the mission that is planned to return people to the lunar surface. The crew will spend the coming months in simulators at Johnson Space Center in Houston, rehearsing every stage of the flight from launch to splashdown.

Much of the training focuses on the landing itself. Two of the astronauts will descend to the surface near the lunar south pole in a commercial lander while the other two remain in orbit aboard the Orion spacecraft. In the simulator, the crew practices landing on terrain models built from orbital imagery, including scenarios where the planned site turns out to be too rough and the crew must divert.

The astronauts are also practicing surface operations in the Neutral Buoyancy Laboratory, a giant pool where they can rehearse moonwalks in pressurized suits. The new suits allow more bending at the waist and knees than the Apollo suits did, which matters for collecting rock samples and working with tools on uneven ground.

Mission planners say the south pole is attractive because some craters there are permanently shadowed and may contain water ice. The crew will collect samples from the edge of one of those regions and deploy instruments to measure the soil's temperature and composition. Engineers have warned that the low sun angle will cast long shadows, making it hard to judge distances.

The timeline remains uncertain. NASA has said the mission depends on test flights of the lander and on further work on the heat shield that protects Orion during reentry. Agency officials told reporters this week that the crew training schedule is designed to keep the astronauts ready even if the launch date moves.

The crew members said they are spending time with geologists to learn how to describe rocks clearly over the radio. One astronaut said the most important skill on the surface will be knowing which samples are worth carrying home.
